# Premium / Paid Support

`customer_support.model.premium_paid_support` · model · parent `—`

> Support is sold as a product with its own price, its own contract and its own renewal. That changes what a support decision is. In every other branch, answering someone quickly out of goodwill is a kindness with no consequence; here it is a discount given away, and it devalues the tier for every customer who paid for the same thing. Generosity stops being free and becomes a pricing action taken by whoever happens to be on the ticket. . The mirror of that, and the branch's characteristic corruption, is that the cheapest way to make the paid tier attractive is to make the unpaid one worse. Nobody decides this. It happens through a hundred defensible small choices — staffing the paid queue first, routing the best agents there, letting the free queue's documentation age — and it is invisible from inside because every individual decision was correct. The only reliable detector is measuring the unpaid experience with the same instruments and the same seriousness as the paid one, which is the first budget cut when the attach rate is under pressure. . The entitlement document becomes a product specification rather than a reference. Customers who paid read it, quote it, and hold the letter of it; every ambiguity is revenue leakage in one direction or a churn event in the other. Scope — what is and is not supported — generates more expensive arguments than technical difficulty ever does, and the skill the branch needs and rarely trains is refusal: saying no clearly, early, with a reason, to somebody who is paying. Agents who cannot refuse deliver unbounded service at a bounded price, and the arithmetic of that shows up two quarters later as a margin problem nobody can attribute. . Breach costs money. Once an SLA carries a credit, missing it is an accounting event with a journal entry, and the incentive to pause the clock becomes financial rather than cosmetic. The pause ledger is now a control that needs auditing, and a support organisation that has never had to defend its own numbers to finance will be surprised by how quickly the metric stops describing reality. . One genuine advantage no other branch has: the customer can cancel support without cancelling the product. That is an early, unambiguous, unmistakable churn signal — a deliberate decision to stop paying for help — and it arrives months before the product renewal it usually precedes. Support non-renewal is the highest-information event in this branch and is normally logged by billing and read by nobody. . What an operator carries over wrongly from an internal cost-centre team: the reflex to absorb. In a cost centre, absorbing an out-of-scope request is efficient — arguing costs more than doing. In a paid tier, absorbing it teaches the customer the scope is negotiable, and the precedent is quoted back at renewal by a procurement team that keeps better records than we do.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| buyer | an IT, engineering or operations leader with a budget line for support specifically, frequently a different person from whoever bought the product and on a different renewal date |
| typical_acv | a defined percentage of product spend or a standalone fee, priced per tier and visibly comparable to competitors' equivalent tiers |
| decision_style | explicit and documented — the tier is chosen against a published matrix, and every promise in that matrix will be tested |
| requester | named, entitled, senior-skewed technical contacts who know exactly what they bought and will cite the clause |
| typical_resolution_hours | 4 |
| volume_shape | moderate volume, high expectation density; the spikes follow the customer's own change windows because premium tiers are bought precisely to cover those |
| staffing_model | a senior-weighted dedicated pool with a hard entitlement gate at intake, sized to the tier's promise rather than to the queue's average |
| coverage | 24x7 for the top tiers, because continuous coverage is the most legible thing a tier can sell |
| automation_level | deliberately low and expensive because of it — what was purchased is a human, and automating the first touch is the fastest way to make the tier feel like the free one |
| primary_channels | `phone`, `ticket_portal`, `chat`, `email` |
| notes | Watch the tier boundary rather than the tier. Almost all of the branch's operational pain concentrates on the customers just below the line they wanted to buy and the ones who bought up a tier and are not using it. The first group generates the scope arguments; the second group churns quietly at renewal having never tested what they paid for, and looks like the healthiest cohort on every dashboard right up until they leave.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `entitled_first_response_minutes`, `entitled_resolution_hours`, `entitled_channels`, `coverage_hours`, `expires_at`


> In this branch the entitlement object is the product specification, and every attribute on it is a clause somebody can quote in an escalation. Nothing may be inferred and nothing may be defaulted: an unresolved entitlement means we do not know what was sold, which is a commercial hole rather than a missing field. `expires_at` matters more here than anywhere else because the support contract can lapse while the product contract runs, and the first ticket after that date is the worst possible moment to discover it.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `is_contractual`, `target_at`, `clock_state`, `credit_exposure`, `pause_reason`, `pause_is_disputable`


> Once a breach carries a credit, the pause ledger becomes a financial control. Every pause is a claim that the delay was the customer's, and `pause_is_disputable` is the attribute that decides whether that claim survives being read back by a customer with the timestamps in front of them. A branch that pauses aggressively will meet its numbers and lose the argument in the room where it matters.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `is_named_account`, `account_arr`, `entitlement_ref`, `sla_target_ref`


> The entitlement reference is mandatory at intake, not at escalation. The whole value of a paid tier is that what may be promised is known before anyone speaks, and the failure mode is an agent making a commitment the tier does not carry — which converts goodwill into a liability that the customer will hold for the rest of the term.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.churn_risk`

Requires `plan_tier`, `renewal_at`, `days_to_renewal`


> The support product renews separately, so it can be cancelled on its own. A downgrade from the top tier is the clearest churn signal available anywhere in this domain: it is deliberate, it is documented, it is taken by a budget holder, and it usually precedes the product renewal by two quarters. It is also almost always invisible to support, because it happens in billing.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `executive_visible`, `reason`, `receiving_owner_ref`


> An escalation from a paying tier is frequently a commercial move rather than a technical one — the customer is establishing a record for the renewal conversation. Reading it as purely technical produces a correct answer to the wrong question. The tell is who is copied: a thread that acquires the customer's procurement or vendor-management function has stopped being about the ticket.

> This branch composes with named_tam and premium is usually where a TAM is sold from, but the two are genuinely separate: a TAM conceded during a renewal is not a priced tier and cannot be withdrawn, whereas everything in this file assumes the service has a number attached. If a tenant matches both, resolve premium first — the entitlement discipline here is the stricter of the two and the TAM branch's informality is what it exists to bound.
